newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Gloom grips gold, U.S. soybeans tumble.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gloom grips gold, U.S. soybeans tumble.

text.p: Gold markets sang the blues again on Monday as bullion languished at a new 4-1/4 year low amid predictions that when the music finally stops prices could be lower still.
Tantalising returns from soaring global stock markets coupled with renewed vigour from the dollar contributed to the general state of despair.
Speculative commodity funds set off the latest wave of selling last week when they began dumping the precious metal from their portfolios on to a reluctant market.
This week's upcoming meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve's monetary policy committee helped keep potential bargain hunters at bay.

Despite a red-hot equities market and thriving U.S. economy, analysts do not expect a change in interest rates. "That suggests there will be no brake put on the stock market so gold can expect to be ignored," one dealer said.
Another noted that bullion could be in the early stages of a two-three year bear market, citing a backdrop of possible gold sales by central banks around the world.

Belgium has announced plans to sell 130 tonnes from its reserves over five years, having already sold 203 tonnes in March last year. Central banks worldwide hold about 35,000 tonnes of the precious metal.
Gold fixed in the morning at $334.05 -- its lowest level since March 30, 1993 -- but recovered slightly to finish the day in London at $334.45 versus $336.65 on Friday.

Elsewhere in the commodity markets, U.S. soybean and soy-derived product prices took a hammering after the Department of Agriculture (USDA) announced it expected U.S. farmers to plant 70.85 million acres (28.7 hectares) of the crop this year -- well above market expectations and the highest since 1982.
November soybean futures at the Chicago Board of Trade hit their daily loss limit when they tumbled 30-cents to trade at $6.17-1/2 per bushel and soyoil sank to a four-year low.

U.S. wheat prices also sold off sharply after the USDA raised its forecast for 1997 spring wheat acreage to roughly 19 million acres versus consensus expectations of 18.1 million acres. Wheat then bounced back and trimmed its losses to just one cent at $3.25 on the July Chicago contract.

On the crude oil front, prices firmed on lingering positive sentiment from last week's announced delay in Iraqi oil exports. The country's former oil sale negotiator, Abdul Amir al-Anbari, said on Friday that oil exports, contingent on United Nations' agreement to an aid distribution plan, may not be resumed until August.
Benchmark Brent crude futures ended the day up $25 in London at $334.35.

World coffee prices bounced higher in late afternoon trade after Brazilian meteorologists said that a polar air mass expected to pass through the country's coffee regions next week could represent the greatest threat of frost so far this year.

But a Smith Barney meteorologist then countered the Brazilian claim by saying that temperatures would not be cold enough to cause any crop damage. September robusta coffee finished up $35 at $1,795, well off its session high of $1,815.
